ops.entry: WHEN a feature's pull request is about to merge DO append and commit your observations log first — the post-merge sweep ships the feature and then removes its worktree, so a log left uncommitted there never reaches the merged branch and can vanish before distillation reads it.
ops.why: The orchestrator log was still uncommitted at merge and survived only because the sweep removes a worktree after the ship record lands. Turns on this repository's post-merge-sweep.py (ship, then feature-worktree remove), so repository tier; Gotchas had a free slot.

ops.entry: WHEN a ruling grants exactly one fix round DO quote its operative wording verbatim in the fix dispatch as the acceptance, and brief the letter rather than the intent — an intent-met fix that misses the letter fails re-validation, and the round it then needs was never granted.
ops.why: One granted round was spent on a fix that met the ruling's intent but not its literal wording (a text-mode read where it said raw bytes), forcing a completion round and a full extra validate dispatch. Displaces G-06, the weakest Gotcha: it turns on one repository's record file and its failure is cheap and self-diagnosing.

originals.original: WHEN an acceptance you hand a lead says the tree must be clean DO exclude the feature record file — run-start and the host token stamp rewrite it during every run, so a clean-tree gate over it fails on the dispatch's own bookkeeping.

ops.entry: WHEN a feature's pull request is about to merge DO leave one orchestrator observation uncommitted in the worktree — the post-merge sweep removes a clean worktree once the ship record lands and keeps a dirty one, and distillation needs the worktree; the distill commit stages the log.
ops.why: Re-judgment: my first G-17 inverted the log bullet and directed committing the log first, which would let the sweep remove the worktree before distill. The worktree survived the ship-record merge because the log was uncommitted; check-state's INV-29 text confirms remove declines on a dirty tree.
